messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For as long as he could remember, Duy had been a man who kept things orderly. At fifty-one, working as a tax inspector for the state, he spent his days in a windowless cubicle reviewing spreadsheets and flagging discrepancies, a profession that rewarded the very meticulousness he had always prided himself on. But order, he had learned, was no protection against what happened in the dark hours of a Tuesday night three years ago.

His wife, Linh, had come home late from a dinner with friends. Duy had asked a simple question—whether she had remembered to file the quarterly estimate—and something in her face had shifted. What followed was a blur, a series of jagged fragments that he could never quite assemble into a coherent whole. He remembered the sting of her open palm against his cheek, the shock that froze him in place. He remembered the heel of her shoe connecting with his ribs as he curled on the kitchen floor. And then, nothing. A gap. A black hole where the next several minutes should have been. He had woken on the tile, alone, with a sharp pain in his side and the taste of blood in his mouth. He never called the police. He never told a soul. He simply got up, cleaned the floor, and went to bed.

In the months that followed, the memory did not stay buried. It forced its way into his mind at the worst moments—while he was driving, while he was trying to focus on a client’s return, while he was lying beside Linh in the dark. The fragments came without warning: the cold tile against his cheek, the sound of her voice, the smell of the dinner she had brought home. Then, just as suddenly, they vanished, leaving him disoriented and ashamed. He had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The world felt flat, drained of possibility. He moved through his days like an object being pushed from task to task, a thing rather than a person. The betrayal was the worst part. He had trusted Linh completely, had built his life around her, and she had broken something fundamental. He was certain now that trust was a trap.

The symptoms bled into every corner of his existence. At work, he began to feel uncomfortable in the open bullpen, exposed and watched. He started arriving early to claim the desk with its back to the wall, and if someone took it first, he would feel a spike of panic so sharp that he would retreat to the bathroom until his heart slowed. He found himself checking over his shoulder whenever he walked to the parking garage, certain that someone was following him even though he knew, rationally, that no one was. At home, unpredictable situations—a sudden knock at the door, Linh’s voice raised on the phone—sent him into a state of hypervigilance. He reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was wrong, his body bracing for a blow that never came.

Fatigue became his constant companion. The exhaustion was not physical so much as total, a bone-deep weariness that made the simplest tasks feel monumental. He stopped meeting his colleagues for lunch, stopped attending his son’s weekend soccer games. He told himself it was because he needed rest, but the truth was that he could not bear the unpredictability of other people—their moods, their movements, their unspoken expectations. He had begun to feel unsafe unless his back was against a wall and he could see the entire room. The consequence was a slow, grinding isolation. His supervisor had pulled him aside twice to ask if everything was all right; Duy had smiled and said he was just tired.

What finally brought him to the clinic was not the fear, nor the exhaustion, nor the memory gaps that still haunted him. It was a single moment, three weeks ago, when his son had asked him to play catch in the backyard. Duy had felt his chest tighten, his throat close. He had said no, and had seen the boy’s face fall. That night, lying awake, he had realized that he was disappearing from his own life. He was terrified of what might happen if he let himself feel the full weight of what Linh had done, but he was even more afraid of what he was becoming—a ghost in his own home. He did not know if he could be put back together, but he had come here, to this room, because he had nowhere else to go.
